title: Amalgamated Meat Cutters v. Connally (1971)
summary: A broad grant of authority to stabilize prices and wages is not an unconstitutional delegation when statutory context, legislative history, an implicit standard of fairness, a short duration, subsidiary administrative standards and judicial review let Congress, the courts and the public tell whether the executive has kept within the legislative will.
notes:
Key line: Judge Leventhal: "When the smoke clears away, however, we conclude that the Rule of Law has been beleaguered but not breached."

Citation: 337 F. Supp. 737 (D.D.C. 1971).

sections.Parties: The plaintiff was the Amalgamated Meat Cutters and Butcher Workmen of North America, AFL-CIO, suing for itself and its affiliated locals. Count I named John B. Connally, Secretary of the Treasury and Chairman of the Cost of Living Council, together with the other cabinet officers and officials who made up the Council, individually and as members. Count II named the major meat packing companies, including Swift, Armour, Hygrade, Wilson, John Morrell and Cudahy, who had refused to pay a bargained wage increase. The federal defendants were represented by the Department of Justice. The case was heard by a three judge district court made up of Circuit Judge Leventhal and District Judges Robinson and Richey, convened because the complaint sought to enjoin enforcement of a federal statute as unconstitutional.
sections.Material Facts: The Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 authorized the President to issue such orders and regulations as he deemed appropriate to stabilize prices, rents, wages and salaries at levels not less than those prevailing on May 25, 1970, with adjustments to prevent gross inequities. A 1971 amendment barred controls on a single industry unless its prices or wages had risen at a grossly disproportionate rate. The Act originally expired in February 1971 and was extended twice for short periods, to April 30, 1972. On August 15, 1971 President Nixon issued Executive Order 11615, freezing prices, rents, wages and salaries for ninety days at the highest levels of the preceding thirty days, exempting raw agricultural products, and creating the Cost of Living Council with all the President's powers under the Act. The union's 1970 contracts called for a twenty five cent hourly raise effective September 6, 1971, which the freeze blocked, and its affiliates had similar increases due for over 150,000 employees.
sections.Procedural History: The union filed a consolidated complaint in the District Court for the District of Columbia. Count II sought to compel the packers to pay the contractual raise; the packers pleaded the Executive Order as a defense. Count I sought a declaration that the Act and the Order were unconstitutional and an injunction against the Council administering them. Because the complaint sought to enjoin a federal statute, a three judge court was convened on October 3, 1971 under 28 U.S.C. 2282 and 2284. It heard argument on the motion for a preliminary injunction on October 8, rejected the Government's threshold claim that the union had an adequate remedy at law, and on October 22, 1971 denied the injunction in an opinion by Judge Leventhal, treating the motion as a determinative ruling on the legal issues because no party contemplated a further evidentiary stage.
sections.Issue: The main question was whether the Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 unconstitutionally delegated legislative power to the President in violation of Article I, Section 1. The union argued that the authority to issue whatever orders he deemed appropriate to stabilize prices and wages was a naked grant with no statement of policy, no requirement of an emergency finding, no fair and equitable standard of the kind found in the 1942 and 1950 statutes, and no provision for administrative procedure or judicial review, so that the President held a blank check. Subsidiary questions were whether the freeze could override existing collective bargaining agreements and whether the words wages and salaries reached fringe benefits.
sections.Holding: The court held that the Act was not an unconstitutional delegation and that the freeze conformed to the legislative will, so the union's facial attack failed and the preliminary injunction was denied. The standards of the Act, read in the context of the 1942 and 1950 stabilization laws and their administration, the House committee report and the floor debates, sufficiently marked the field so that a court could tell whether the will of Congress had been obeyed. The court also read the Act to contain an implicit standard of broad fairness and avoidance of gross inequity, to require the executive to develop subsidiary administrative standards, and to be subject to the rulemaking and judicial review provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act. Existing contracts did not fetter Congress, and fringe benefits were within the stabilization power.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Leventhal took Yakus v. United States rather than Schechter and Panama Refining as the guide. The Constitution does not forbid every delegation; the question is one of limits, and the test is whether Congress has laid down an intelligible principle so that Congress, the courts and the public can tell whether the agency has kept within the legislative will. The 1970 Act was not tested in a vacuum. It set a floor at May 25, 1970 levels, barred singling out an industry without a finding of disproportionate increases, and was enacted against the background of two prior stabilization programs whose freeze and hold the line techniques supplied a common lore of what stabilization meant. The House report explained why Congress delegated the timing of controls: it believed cost push inflation required direct controls that the President had refused, so it created standby authority. The Act's short life, renewed every few months, gave Congress close control and denied it the option of acquiescence by inaction. Reading the statute to avoid constitutional doubt and in light of its history, it found an implicit duty of broad fairness and avoidance of gross inequity, a requirement that the executive develop implementing standards that would then confine later action, and full applicability of the APA, since the Council was an agency and Congress had not exempted the Act. Judicial review was therefore available beyond enforcement proceedings.

topics.lrs-s-accountability: The court relied on implicit fairness, temporary authority, administrative standards, and judicial review; the editors questioned their practical effectiveness.
topics.lrs-s-avoidance: The court resisted a reading that would confer power to act unfairly, partly to avoid serious constitutional doubt.
topics.lrs-s-agency-self-limitation: Leventhal relied on the executive's duty to develop standards that would then bind it as a constraint saving the broad delegation.
topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: The court upheld the Economic Stabilization Act against a nondelegation challenge, reading statutory context, time limits and judicial review as supplying the required principle.

learning.why: The course assigns it as the fullest modern judicial statement of why the intelligible principle test tolerates very broad delegations, and for its method of finding constraints in statutory context, duration, self imposed administrative standards and judicial review rather than in the text alone.
